title: DNA-linked inhibitor antibody assay (DIANA): An advanced method for screening influenza endonuclease inhibitors.
abstract: Influenza virus endonuclease cleaves host cell-capped RNA, an essential step in acquiring primers for initiation of viral transcription. Currently, one endonuclease inhibitor, baloxavir marboxil (marketed as Xofluza), is approved for clinical use, and others are under development. Development of new antivirals could be expedited by simple, cost-effective screening methods. We previously introduced a multiwell plate-based DNA-linked inhibitor antibody assay (DIANA) capable of detecting enzyme at femtomolar concentrations. DIANA has also been applied for high-throughput inhibitor screening, enabling determination of equilibrium inhibition constants (Ki) from single-well measurements. Here, we set out to extend DIANA to influenza endonuclease, to obtain standardized Ki values for a structurally diverse panel of known inhibitors and benchmark them against orthogonal assays, and to apply the resulting assay to a newly designed series of inhibitors built on a more synthetically accessible scaffold. To this end, we present the design and synthesis of an L-742,001 derivative linked to a reporter DNA oligonucleotide for use in DIANA. The endonuclease is captured by an immobilized antibody, and test compounds compete with the oligo-linked detection probe for binding to the enzyme, which is quantified by qPCR. DIANA was validated using a focused panel of influenza endonuclease inhibitors and benchmarked against AlphaScreen and differential scanning fluorimetry, with the three methods showing broadly consistent structure-activity relationship (SAR) trends. Finally, we designed, synthesized, and evaluated a focused library of hydroxypyrimidinone derivatives. The hydroxypyrimidinone scaffold retained potent endonuclease inhibition while offering a more synthetically accessible alternative to hydroxypyridinones, supporting its use for systematic SAR exploration.

title: Loss of replication and transcription systems accompanying transition to nucleus-dependent replication in "Ariadnavirales", a proposed new order in nucleocytoviricot class Megaviricetes.
abstract: Sicyoidochytrium minutum DNA virus (SmDNAV) was isolated several years ago from a protist host of family Thraustochytriaceae of the class Labyrinthulomycetes. This virus shared little similarity to other viruses in gene content and protein sequences, albeit seemingly belonging to the phylum Nucleocytoviricota . By extensive searches in genomic and metagenomic sequence databases, we identified numerous long contigs related to the SmDNAV genome and analyzed proteins shared by these putative viruses. Phylogenetic analyses place these viruses within the class Megaviricetes , outside of all established orders, and as a sister group to the clade combining families Mamonoviridae and " Manesviridae ". Homologs of SmDNAV proteins were found in association (either integrated or co-sequenced) with other Labyrinthulomycetes and Rhodophyta protists from diverse marine and freshwater environments. Consequently, we propose SmDNAV as the prototype member of a new order, provisionally named "Ariadnavirales", within class Megaviricetes , phylum Nucleocytoviricota . Members of "Ariadnavirales" have lost most of the genes encoding components of the replication and transcription systems that are otherwise conserved in nucleocytoviricots, suggestive of transition to genome replication and expression dependent on the host nucleus. The viral phylum Nucleocytoviricota consists of diverse viruses with double-stranded DNA genomes within a broad size range from about 40 kilobases to about 5 megabases. The great majority of nucleocytoviricots encode DNA and RNA polymerases, and other proteins involved in genome replication and expression, and are known or predicted to replicate within viral 'factories' in the host cell cytoplasm. In recent years, several new groups of nucleocytoviricots have been discovered, primarily, by metagenome mining. Here we describe a putative new order of nucleocytoviricots, which we provisionally name "Ariadnavirales" for their protist hosts. These viruses have lost most of the genes responsible for genome replication and expression in other nucleocytoviricots, and their replication apparently depends on the host nucleus.

title: BCLAF1-Mediated Regulation of RNA Processing and the DNA Damage Response and Its Cancer-Related Implications.
abstract: BCLAF1 (Bcl-2-associated transcription factor 1) was initially identified as a Bcl-2-interacting nuclear protein, and early studies mainly placed it in the context of transcriptional repression and apoptosis. As its interaction network has become clearer, BCLAF1 is now viewed as a multifunctional protein linking RNA processing, the DNA damage response and cell fate regulation. Current evidence shows that BCLAF1 contributes to splicing, nuclear export and expression maintenance of repair-related transcripts and is functionally linked to DNA damage response complexes, thereby influencing DNA repair efficiency and post-damage cell fate decisions. In cancer, BCLAF1 acts in a context-dependent manner: in some settings it supports hypoxic adaptation, metabolic reprogramming, immune evasion and therapy resistance, whereas in others it is associated with genome stability and tissue homeostasis. Its functional output depends on splicing isoforms, subcellular localization, post-translational modifications, interaction networks and cellular state. This review discusses the structural features, spatial localization, post-translational regulation, regulation at the DDR-RNA metabolism interface, cancer-related roles and translational limitations of BCLAF1.

title: CRISPR-Cas gene regulation in mycobacteria: From single-gene targeting to dynamic network rewiring.
abstract: Mycobacteria represent both clinically important pathogens and valuable microbial chassis, creating a demand for precise and scalable gene-regulatory technologies. However, conventional genetic approaches suffer from inefficient recombination, lengthy strain construction, and restricted capacity for multiplex manipulation. The application of diverse CRISPR-Cas systems in mycobacterial genetics has substantially expanded the genetic toolbox available for these organisms, enabling programmable genome editing and transcriptional regulation. Among these platforms, Cas9-based systems have facilitated essential-gene interrogation and resistance-associated genetic screens; however, their broader application is constrained by protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) dependence, DNA-break-associated toxicity, and limited multiplex capability. Cas12-family effectors, characterized by their distinct PAM preferences, compact architectures, and intrinsic CRISPR RNA (crRNA) processing capacity, provide alternative strategies for expanding target accessibility and regulatory scalability. Here, we critically review the development of CRISPR-based regulatory platforms in mycobacteria, focusing on the transition from the Cas9-centered single-gene manipulation toward the Cas12-enabled multiplex and network-level regulation. We discuss emerging miniature effectors and dynamic regulatory modules that may overcome current limitations in target coverage, temporal control, and host compatibility. Finally, we highlight key engineering challenges and future directions toward programmable regulatory systems integrating protein engineering, synthetic biology, and spatiotemporal control, with potential applications in tuberculosis research and mycobacterial metabolic engineering.

title: Draft genome sequence data of a chitin-degrading bacterium, Flavivirga sp. 57AJ16, isolated from intertidal sediment of the Yellow Sea, China.
abstract: Flavivirga sp. 57AJ16, a chitin-degrading bacterium, was isolated from intertidal sediment collected from the Yellow Sea of China using a long-term enrichment strategy with colloidal chitin. Here, we report the draft genome sequence and genomic features of strain 57AJ16. Whole-genome sequencing was performed on the Illumina NovaSeq platform with 150 bp paired-end sequencing. The assembled genome comprised 4,920,416 bp with a guanine-cytosine (GC) content of 34.5%, containing 4,076 predicted protein-coding genes, 38 transfer RNA (tRNA) genes, and 3 ribosomal RNA (rRNA) genes. Genome-based annotation identified one putative glycoside hydrolase family 18 (GH18) chitinase and three glycoside hydrolase family 20 (GH20) proteins, including two putative β-hexosaminidases, potentially associated with chitin utilization. Phylogenetic analyses based on the 16S rRNA gene and genome-wide core orthologous proteins placed strain 57AJ16 within the genus Flavivirga. Average nucleotide identity analysis showed relatively low genomic similarity between strain 57AJ16 and the currently available Flavivirga genomes, indicating that strain 57AJ16 represents a genomically differentiated lineage within the genus Flavivirga. However, the available genomic and phylogenetic evidence is insufficient to formally propose strain 57AJ16 as a novel species. This genome provides a reference for comparative analysis of chitin-degrading Flavivirga strains. Raw sequencing reads have been deposited in the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) Sequence Read Archive (SRA) under BioProject accession number PRJNA1469928. The genome sequence has been deposited in DDBJ/EMBL/GenBank under accession number JAQZAT000000000, and the 16S rRNA gene sequence has been deposited under accession number OQ348283.

title: Role and mechanism of long chain noncoding RNA-mediated TCF7-AURKA axis in regulating foam cell macrophages in coronary heart disease.
abstract: To explore the role and mechanism of the long non-coding RNA (lncRNA)-mediated TCF7-AURKA axis in macrophage foam cell formation and the progression of coronary heart disease. Foam cell models were established using THP-1 cells and primary monocyte-derived macrophages. LncRNA, TCF7, or AURKA were silenced individually, with PI3K/AKT/mTOR inhibitors used for intervention. Lipid quantification was performed using Oil Red O staining and high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). Dil-oxLDL uptake was detected by flow cytometry. Protein and mRNA expressions were measured using western blot and qRT-PCR, and AURKA activity was evaluated with a kinase assay kit. Cholesterol efflux, inflammatory factor levels (ELISA), and Transwell migration were also assessed. Silencing the lncRNA-TCF7-AURKA axis significantly reduced foam cell lipid accumulation (cholesterol ester [CE]: 42% decrease; CE/free cholesterol [FC] ratio: 35% decrease), diminished oxLDL uptake (30% reduction), inhibited PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway phosphorylation, enhanced autophagy (increased LC3 and decreased P62), promoted ApoA-1-mediated cholesterol efflux (32% increase), downregulated IL-1β and TNF-α (25% reduction each), and impaired cell migration. These effects were verified in primary cells, with AURKA kinase activity decreasing by 45%. The lncRNA-TCF7-AURKA axis activates the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway to inhibit autophagy, thereby promoting lipid deposition and inflammation. This is a key pathway driving macrophage foam cell formation and atherosclerosis, providing a theoretical basis for combined targeted intervention.

title: Ancestral Quadruplication of Protein Kinase R in Tarsiers Hints Towards Novel Primate-Virus Innovations.
abstract: Tarsiers, an elusive family of primates found in Indonesia and the Philippines, sit at an essential point in primate evolution, with their divergence between that of Strepsirrhini (lemurs) and Simiiformes (monkeys and apes). Through homology searches, we have discovered that tarsiers carry the first known case in primates of a gene expansion of protein kinase R (PKR), a kinase involved in the response to viral infection. PKR was quadruplicated in the ancestor of tarsiers and has been maintained since then in all sequenced tarsier species. The extra copies lack the double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) binding domains necessary for detecting viral infection yet largely maintain the residues necessary for the kinase function that carries out PKR's antiviral function. We show that three of the four PKR copies indeed maintain kinase activity, one of which appears to be resistant to the viral PKR antagonist K3 from vaccinia virus. Our analyses of site and branch-site positive selection reveal that the tarsier PKRs are under positive selection. We propose that these extra copies could serve as a diversification strategy to bypass viral inhibitors that bind PKR's kinase domain, or they could alternatively serve as decoys that shield the canonical PKR from viral inhibition. This is the first instance of mammal PKR duplicates lacking dsRNA-binding domains and may highlight an innovation in an ancient, long-standing molecular arms race between viruses and a close relative of humans.

title: From prophylaxis to precision immunotherapy via engineering vaccine platforms.
abstract: Vaccines are evolving from antigen-delivery products into modular technologies designed to elicit specific immune functions. Although prophylactic vaccination aims to establish protective memory before exposure, therapeutic vaccination must redirect immunity in the presence of persistent antigen, immune suppression or pathological tissue remodeling. In this Review, we examine how antigen architecture, innate sensing, antigen-presenting-cell targeting, platform design and administration route jointly determine vaccine-induced immune programmes. We compare the distinct requirements of prevention and treatment, focusing on cancer, chronic viral infection and fibrosis, and assess the opportunities and limitations of RNA vaccines, viral vectors, virus-like particles, adjuvants and combination strategies. We then consider how systems vaccinology and artificial intelligence can inform immunogen design and response prediction, while distinguishing computational promise from experimentally validated benefit. We argue that clinical progress depends on matching each vaccine formulation to a defined biological barrier and demonstrating tissue-level activity, safety, durability and practical deployability. This framework connects vaccine engineering to measurable protective or therapeutic outcomes without assuming that any single platform is universally optimal. By integrating immunological principles with advances in vaccine engineering, this Review provides a conceptual basis for selecting and combining technologies according to disease-specific requirements. Ultimately, this perspective may help guide the development of more precise, adaptable and clinically relevant vaccination strategies, bridging the gap between platform innovation and improved outcomes in prevention and therapy.

title: Structure of the marsupial IGF2R locus.
abstract: The insulin-like growth factor 2 receptor gene (IGF2R) is a maternally-expressed developmental regulator in therian mammals, eutherians and marsupials. In mice the paternal allele of Igf2r is silenced by transcriptional overlap from a ~108 kb antisense Igf2r RNA (Airn) expressed from a differentially methylated region (DMR) in intron 2. In tammar wallabies there is also an antisense transcript (ALID), but it is short, ~650 bp, and it is transcribed from a DMR in intron 12. Here, the structure of the IGF2R DMR and ALID was investigated to evaluate its evolutionary similarity across mammals. A lack of sequence similarity between the intragenic CpG island in eutherians (euCGI-2) and marsupials (maCGI-2) suggested independent acquisition in each lineage. In tammars, maCGI-2 had active histone marks and promoter activity. Transcription from maCGI-2 was complex, with multiple sense and antisense transcripts. Low-level detection of a long-ALID transcript supported a model in which IGF2R imprinting is achieved by transcriptional overlap in marsupials as in eutherians. The maCGI-2 had CTCF sites and was a boundary for 3D interactions with the IGF2R start site and a broader domain containing the maternally-expressed SLC22A3 gene ~250 kb away. These findings indicate that maCGI-2 is a site of complex transcriptional regulation and is a structurally important feature within IGF2R and the broader region.

title: Time-resolved multi-omics reveals sustained antiviral activation and hepatic lipid remodeling during ALV-J infection in chickens.
abstract: Avian leukosis virus subgroup J (ALV-J) is an oncogenic retrovirus associated with persistent infection, immunosuppression, and neoplastic diseases in chickens, with the liver serving as an important target organ. However, the temporal coordination of hepatic immune and metabolic responses during the early course of ALV-J infection remains unclear. Here, we performed time-resolved proteomic and metabolomic analyses of chicken livers at 7, 14, and 21 days post-infection (dpi). Hepatic ALV-J RNA was detected throughout the observation period and was accompanied by histopathological injury and extensive immunometabolic remodeling. Antiviral and interferon-responsive proteins, including OASL, STAT1, EIF2AK2, and CMPK2, remained elevated at multiple time points. The sustained elevation of these antiviral proteins was accompanied by reductions in selected mitochondrial respiratory-chain proteins and the redox cofactors NADH and flavin mononucleotide. Lipid remodeling also became increasingly prominent over the course of infection, as reflected by the accumulation of multiple lysophospholipid species, together with decreases in phospholipid backbone-related metabolites. Based on its persistent induction and known roles in antiviral responses and mitochondrial nucleotide metabolism, CMPK2 was selected for functional analysis. ALV-J infection induced CMPK2 expression in HD11 cells. CMPK2 overexpression increased intracellular DHE fluorescence, ALV-J Env protein levels, and infectious viral titers, whereas treatment with CMPK2-targeting siRNAs reduced DHE fluorescence without significantly affecting viral replication. These findings suggest that CMPK2 contributes to infection-associated changes in DHE fluorescence in HD11 cells, while its overexpression can enhance ALV-J replication under the tested conditions. Collectively, the early course of ALV-J infection is characterized by sustained antiviral activation accompanied by mitochondrial/redox and hepatic phospholipid remodeling, with CMPK2 representing a potential contributor to the associated oxidative response.

title: Electroacupuncture Alleviates Neuropathic Pain in Rats by Regulating the Camk4-Ehmt2/G9a-Oprm1 Axis.
abstract: Neuropathic pain (NP) is a common type of chronic pain in clinical practice, for which current therapeutic options remain limited. Electroacupuncture (EA) shows promising therapeutic potential, but its underlying molecular mechanisms are yet to be fully elucidated. A rat model of NP was established by chronic constriction injury (CCI) of the sciatic nerve, and pain behaviors were assessed by measuring paw withdrawal thresholds to mechanical stimuli. EA was applied to the ipsilateral acupoints Zusanli (ST36) and Yanglingquan (GB34). Pharmacological inhibitors, high-throughput RNA sequencing, Western blotting, and qRT-PCR were comprehensively employed to explore the molecular mechanisms underlying EA-induced relief of NP. EA significantly attenuated mechanical hypersensitivity in CCI rats. On day 14, EA significantly increased the 50% PWT compared with both BC (P < 0.0001) and SA (P < 0.05) (no significant change was observed in the sham group). Mechanistically, the previously reported DS-LncRNA in mice was not detected in the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) of CCI rats. Instead, EA significantly upregulated Camk4 and Oprm1 and downregulated Ehmt2/G9a at both mRNA and protein levels compared with BC (P < 0.001) and SA (P < 0.05)(except sham group), and these changes were associated with alleviation of NP progression. EA alleviates NP in CCI rats by regulating the Camk4-Ehmt2/G9a-Oprm1 axis, including upregulation of Camk4 and suppression of Ehmt2/G9a-mediated repression of Oprm1. Camk4 and Ehmt2/G9a may serve as potential novel therapeutic targets for NP management; however, the BRD4770-induced partial restoration of Camk4 suggests possible feedback regulation between Ehmt2/G9a and Camk4, whether Camk4 directly and causally regulates Ehmt2/G9a requires further rescue experiments.

title: Hepatocellular Tumors in Patients With Ornithine Transcarbamylase Deficiency Include Focal Nodular Hyperplasia, Hepatocellular Adenoma, and Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
abstract: Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency (OTCD) is the most common urea cycle disorder and can cause potentially life-threatening hyperammonemia. Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and hepatocellular adenoma (HCA) have been reported in OTCD, usually in adults. Non-neoplastic histologic findings include non-specific glycogenosis, steatosis, and fibrosis. A retrospective pathology database search between 2000 and 2024 was performed to identify patients with a clinical history of OTCD. Electronic medical records were reviewed for clinical, laboratory, genetic, and imaging findings. Available native liver specimens underwent histologic review, with additional studies performed in select cases. We identified 11 patients with OTCD. All patients were diagnosed biochemically; pathogenic OTC mutations were detected in all 8 tested patients. Three patients had hepatocellular lesions. One patient with Li-Fraumeni syndrome developed focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH) at age 6 and conventional HCC at age 10, when OTCD was also diagnosed. RNA sequencing revealed biased allelic expression toward the mutant OTC allele in the FNH (100% mutant), HCC (94% mutant), and background liver (87% mutant). Two additional pediatric patients had incidental HCAs identified on explant examination at 9 and 17 years of age. The remaining 8 patients (72%) had no focal hepatic lesions. Glycogenosis was the most common histologic finding (10/11, 91%). Only 1 patient had significant steatosis (grade 2) or fibrosis (stage 1). Hepatocellular tumors in OTCD included HCC, HCA, and FNH in pediatric patients. Glycogenosis was the predominant non-neoplastic histologic finding. These findings expand the spectrum of hepatic lesions and non-neoplastic liver pathology reported in OTCD.

title: ChIP-seq analysis of SMAD3 target genes in a sea anemone reveals symbiosis-dependent regulation through TGF-β signaling
abstract: Background: Cnidarian-algal symbiosis underpins coral reefs, but elevated temperatures can disrupt it, causing bleaching. Bleaching activates host stress and immune pathways and disrupts symbiotic signaling and nutrient transfer. Among these pathways, the immunosuppressive cytokine transforming growth factor-{beta} (TGF-{beta}) promotes host tolerance of symbionts in cnidarians, but the genes regulated by its transcription factor, SMAD3, remain unknown. SMAD3 ChIP-seq and RNA-seq were used to identify putative targets in symbiotic and aposymbiotic Exaiptasia diaphana after 6 and 18 h of heat stress. Results: SMAD3 binding was highly specific to each combination of symbiotic state and heat treatment. Symbiotic state, not heat stress, drove most differential binding, with binding nearly always higher in symbiotic animals. Integration identified 625 putative targets differentially bound and expressed between symbiotic states. Differential binding between symbiotic states peaked at 18 h, when these targets made up the largest share of symbiosis-associated expression differences. Activation targets suggest SMAD3 supports symbiosis through the mucociliary surface, host control of nitrogen available to symbionts, uptake of symbiont-derived retinoids, and immunity. Repression targets, which outnumbered activation targets at 18 h, suggest SMAD3 limits canonical sterol transport, alters G protein-coupled receptor expression, and may reinforce its own activity by repressing negative regulators of TGF-{beta} signaling. Conclusions: SMAD3 appears to act as a bifunctional regulator whose binding is shaped primarily by symbiotic state. Its putative targets suggest roles in cnidarian symbiosis beyond immune suppression, including nutrient exchange and retinoid signaling. These findings provide a framework for TGF-{beta} function in cnidarian symbiosis and thermal stress.

title: Salivary-based protein and RNA biomarkers as early diagnostic Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Progressive neuronal degeneration is one of the symptoms of neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs), which often cause cognitive and physical impairments. In order to start therapy before clinical symptoms appear and to limit the progression of diseases like Parkinson's disease (PD) and Alzheimer's disease (AD), early screening and diagnosis are crucial. Finding new, accurate and reliable biomarkers is a key objective in recent research in order to facilitate early diagnosis and offer insights into the progression of disease. Compared with invasive, complex, and costly cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) screening methods, salivary analysis has emerged as a promising approach for identifying biomarkers and matrices relevant to assessing NDDs. Compared to other often examined biofluids, saliva collection offers a number of benefits due to its accessibility, non-invasiveness, and suitability for recurrent sampling. These characteristics facilitate early diagnosis and timely treatment of diseases. Current research indicates that β-amyloid (Aβ), tau protein, alpha synuclein (α-syn), DJ-1, and several miRNAs in saliva show potential as biomarkers for neurodegenerative diseases. This narrative review addresses the growing need for reliable and standardized saliva-based biomarkers by integrating evidence on biomarker performance with methodological challenges, emerging technologies, and innovative perspectives on multimarker panels, standardization, and validation to facilitate their clinical translation in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases.

title: Multi-omics analysis links Lycium barbarum glycopeptide-mediated retinal protection to glycolytic remodeling and protein lactylation in retinitis pigmentosa models.
abstract: Lycium barbarum L. (goji, wolfberry) is a traditional Chinese medicinal and food plant long associated with nourishment and ocular health. Lycium barbarum glycopeptide (LbGP), a purified glycopeptide fraction derived from Lycium barbarum polysaccharides, has shown retinal and neuroprotective potential, but its metabolic mechanism in inherited retinal degeneration remains unclear. To determine whether LbGP treatment is associated with glycolytic remodeling, lactate metabolism, and protein lactylation in experimental models of retinitis pigmentosa (RP). Public single-cell RNA sequencing data from PRPF31-mutant and control human retinal organoids were integrated with retinal proteomic, lactylomic, and metabolomic datasets from wild-type, vehicle-treated rd10, and LbGP-treated rd10 mice. Findings were examined using lactate measurement, ATP detection, pan-lysine lactylation immunofluorescence, cell viability assays, Western blotting, retinal structural assessment, and dark-adapted electroretinography. PRPF31-mutant photoreceptors showed increased glycolysis- and hypoxia-related transcription with reduced phototransduction and oxidative phosphorylation. In rd10 retinas, LbGP treatment was associated with changes in glycolysis-related enzymes, disease-associated lysine lactylation, and energy-related metabolites. Integrated multi-omics analysis nominated a glycolysis-lactate-lactylation axis involving selected glycolytic enzymes and Kla sites. LbGP increased the viability of serum-deprived 661W cells and preserved retinal structure and function in rd10 mice. It also increased the lactate production in both 661W cells and rd10 retinas. The ATP levels, pan-lysine lactylation, and the expression of PFKP and LDHA were increased by LbGP treatment in serum-deprived 661W cells, with the effect partially blocked by HK1 inhibitor 2-DG. Glycolytic remodeling and protein lactylation may represent candidate mechanisms associated with LbGP-mediated retinal protection in RP models, supporting further pharmacological validation of LbGP as a Lycium barbarum-derived intervention for retinal degeneration.

title: Precision drug delivery for ulcerative colitis: engineering the colonic microenvironment for site-specific and responsive therapy.
abstract: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic, relapsing inflammatory bowel disease characterised by continuous inflammation and ulceration of the colonic mucosa, resulting from complex interactions among genetic susceptibility, environmental factors, intestinal barrier dysfunction, gut microbiota dysbiosis, and dysregulated immune responses. Although conventional therapies, including aminosalicylates, corticosteroids, immunomodulators, biologics, and small-molecule drugs have improved disease control, their clinical utility remains limited by incomplete therapeutic responses, adverse effects, loss of efficacy, and difficulties in achieving sustained remission. The present review offers an in-depth view of the emerging trends in molecular pharmacology and future drug-delivery systems for UC. UC-relevant molecular targets and pathological features of the colonic microenvironment be matched to site-specific or stimulus-responsive delivery strategies to improve local therapeutic exposure while limiting systemic toxicity, and clinical translation have been described. We discuss recent therapeutic advances targeting key inflammatory pathways (e.g. TNF-α, JAK-STAT, TYK2, IL-23/Th17, S1P receptors and PPAR-γ) and microbiome-directed approaches (e.g. faecal microbiota transplantation, microbial metabolites and postbiotics). Biomarker-driven approaches, such as faecal calprotectin and microbiota profiling, are emphasised as key components of precision medicine and treatment monitoring. Advanced Drug delivery mechanisms such as liposomes, polymeric nanoparticles, solid lipid nanoparticles, hydrogels, microparticles, nanogels and multifunctional theranostic systems provide opportunities for colon-specific drug delivery, controlled release, improved bioavailability, improved mucosal targeting and decreased systemic exposure. New approaches based on RNA-based therapeutics, CRISPR/Cas technologies and artificial intelligence-assisted drug delivery system design further increase the possibilities of personalised treatment. To summarise, the combination of molecularly targeted pharmacology with intelligent and site-specific drug-delivery technologies is an exciting avenue for enhancing therapeutic efficacy and reducing treatment-related toxicity and for furthering personalised management of UC. However, translation to widespread clinical practice will need to overcome challenges related to biocompatibility, gastrointestinal variability, scalability, manufacturing, controlled release, and regulatory approval.

title: Intermediate Densification of Collagen Hydrogels Promotes Fibrocartilage-Like Tendon-Bone Healing.
abstract: Regeneration of the fibrocartilaginous tendon-bone enthesis remains a challenge because scar tissue often replaces the functional transitional interface. Biomaterial scaffolds can provide physical cues for interface regeneration, but conventional collagen hydrogels have sparse fibrillar networks and low stiffness. Here, graded plastic compression co-tuned collagen density, pore area fraction, degradation behavior, and multiscale stiffness within a chemically unchanged collagen I system. The target reductions in initial gel thickness were 0% (non-compressed, NC), 50% (low-compression, LC), 70% (moderate-compression, MC), and 90% (high-compression, HC). Material properties changed progressively across these conditions, whereas bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cell (BMSC) responses were non-monotonic. MC was the first condition to show a marked increase in bulk stiffness, with corresponding local stiffening, while remaining less compact than HC; it also produced the most favorable overall proliferation, fibrocartilage-associated marker expression, and matrix deposition among the four conditions tested. RNA sequencing revealed MC-associated transcriptional programs related to the cell cycle, cartilage development, extracellular matrix organization, and candidate mechanosensing processes. Pharmacological FAK inhibition reduced MC-associated FAK phosphorylation, YAP1 nuclear localization, and SOX9 expression without a measurable change in total integrin β1 fluorescence intensity, supporting a FAK-sensitive contribution within the YAP1/SOX9 response. In a rat rotator cuff repair model, the selected MC construct improved gait and mechanical properties and promoted more organized fibrocartilage-like interface remodeling compared with the control conditions. These findings identify an intermediate densification physical window within the tested collagen I series and establish graded compression as a practical strategy for selecting collagen constructs for tendon-bone repair. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Rotator cuff repair rarely restores the fibrocartilaginous tendon-bone interface. Existing biomaterial studies often vary scaffold composition, bioactive signals, and physical properties together, making the contribution of matrix physical state difficult to define. By applying graded plastic compression to a compositionally constant type I collagen system, this study identifies an intermediate densification window that outperforms both minimally and maximally compressed matrices in supporting mesenchymal stem cell proliferation and fibrocartilage-associated differentiation. Transcriptomic profiling and pharmacological inhibition further support a FAK-sensitive contribution to the YAP1/SOX9 response. The selected construct also improves gait, mechanical properties, and interface organization in vivo. These findings reveal a non-monotonic structure-function relationship and provide a broadly relevant physical design principle for regenerative biomaterials and tendon-bone repair.

title: Hypoxia reprograms tRNA cleavage toward 5'-halves in trophoblasts: convergent Glu-tRF enrichment in syncytiotrophoblast vesicles during preeclampsia.
abstract: Preeclampsia (PE) is characterized by placental ischaemia and a massive release of syncytiotrophoblast extracellular vesicles (STB-EVs). Transfer RNA-derived fragments (tRFs) form a substantial fraction of STB-EV RNA, but the mechanisms of their biogenesis and selective sorting under hypoxia remain unclear. To profile the tRF pool in placental tissue and STB-EVs in PE, alongside in vitro hypoxia in BeWo b30 cells, and to validate specific stress-induced tRFs. We re-analysed small RNA-seq from placental tissue and STB-EV fractions from normotensive and PE pregnancies, and from BeWo b30 treated with CoCl2 or a selective HIF-1α stabiliser (the oxyquinoline derivative neuradapt). Candidate tRFs were validated by RT-qPCR in cells and EVs. In vitro hypoxia reprogrammed small RNA processing in trophoblasts: Dicer-dependent microRNAs decreased, angiogenin (ANG) was strongly induced, and 32-33-nt 5' tRNA halves accumulated. In clinical samples, PE was associated with compartment-specific tRF changes: placental tissue showed modest remodelling, whereas STB-EVs displayed increased 5'-halves and altered tRF cleavage positions. Specific glutamate tRFs (Glu-tRFs) were consistently enriched in STB-EVs. RT-qPCR confirmed that chemical hypoxia induces 32-33-nt Glu-tRF 5'-halves in cells and promotes their selective loading into EVs. Rank-based analysis indicated that Glu-tRF sorting into STB-EVs depends on fragment structural features and is associated with stress-induced changes in the RNA-binding protein YBX1. Placental hypoxia triggers ANG-dependent biogenesis of 5' Glu-tRNA halves and their selective export in STB-EVs. The convergent fragments identified here, particularly 10_GluTTC_33 and 13_GluTTC_33, are promising non-invasive biomarkers of placental ischaemia and candidate paracrine effectors in PE.

title: Integrated multiscale profiling of light-dependent physiological and molecular responses in Chlorobaculum tepidum, a model green sulfur bacterium.
abstract: Chlorobaculum tepidum and other green sulfur bacteria thrive in extreme low-light environments, yet the molecular basis of light acclimation remains unclear. Using optical spectroscopy, electron microscopy, RNA sequencing, and data-independent acquisition (DIA) proteomics, we characterized C. tepidum grown under high, medium, and low light. Growth increased with light, with high-light cells undergoing anisotropic elongation. Bacteriochlorophyll c per cell was comparable under medium and high light, whereas low-light cultures exhibited declining optical density, indicating a substantially different physiological state from the actively growing cultures. The BChl c Qy absorption maximum was unchanged across conditions, consistent with adjustment of antenna abundance rather than pigment organization. Transcriptomics revealed a coordinated, low-light-biased upregulation of light-harvesting, sulfur oxidation, and carbon fixation genes, with sulfur metabolism genes most enriched. DIA proteomics expanded the known proteome and uncovered extensive transcript-protein decoupling, with pigment-biosynthetic enzymes unaffected despite shifting pigment levels. These data establish a two-axis model where antenna remodeling and compensatory sulfur metabolism operate over a stable, post-transcriptionally controlled proteome.

title: NG2/CSPG4 integrates matrix-derived signaling to coordinate osteochondral adaptation during temporomandibular joint health and disease.
abstract: Post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA) of the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) involves extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling and altered cell-matrix interactions. Type VI collagen is a component of the mandibular condylar cartilage pericellular matrix, where it interacts with neuron-glial antigen 2 (NG2/CSPG4). We investigated how NG2/CSPG4 deficiency influences ECM-associated communication, chondrocyte transcriptional programs, and osteochondral architecture during TMJ PTOA. Single-cell RNA sequencing and CellChat analyses identified chondrocytes as prominent contributors to ECM-associated communication during PTOA, including COLLAGEN, FN1, SPP1, and THBS pathways. Compared with wild-type controls, NG2/CSPG4 knockout (NG2ko) tissues exhibited increased predicted communication, particularly through COLLAGEN, FN1, and THBS pathways, with enhanced predicted COL6A2-SDC4 interactions within cartilaginous cells. NG2ko chondrocytes showed increased expression of collagen VI and other cartilage matrix genes alongside reduced hypertrophy- and matrix remodeling-associated transcriptional signatures. Increased Smad3 expression and its connectivity within a protein interaction network suggested a potential role for SMAD3-associated regulation. Microcomputed tomography revealed persistently reduced subchondral trabecular number and increased bone volume during later PTOA progression, while histological analyses demonstrated reduced cartilage nuclear density. Together, these findings indicate that NG2/CSPG4 deficiency reorganizes ECM-associated communication and chondrocyte transcriptional programs while altering cartilage and subchondral bone architecture. NG2/CSPG4 may therefore contribute to coordination of cell-matrix interactions and osteochondral responses to injury.

title: Zucchini yellow mosaic virus (ZYMV) in Cucurbit crops: global advances, China-specific evidence and integrated management.
abstract: Zucchini yellow mosaic virus (ZYMV), a member of the genus Potyvirus, is primarily transmitted via aphids and seeds. Causing severe symptoms such as leaf mosaic, plant stunting, and fruit deformation, ZYMV has emerged as a major constraint to the development of Cucurbita crop industries in China. Although early studies have documented its occurrence in certain regions, a systematic understanding of its epidemiological patterns and management in major Cucurbita crops is urgently needed. This review comprehensively synthesizes the biological and genomic characteristics, epidemiology, host-virus interactions, and detection technologies of ZYMV in China, with the aim of integrating effective management strategies. Current evidence suggests that Chinese ZYMV populations exhibit regional genetic variation and possible recombination events, although nationwide population structure and the ecological contribution of non-crop reservoirs remain insufficiently resolved. Variations in coat protein (CP), helper component-proteinase (HC-Pro) and protein 3 (P3) have been associated with differences in symptom expression or transmission in particular virus-host systems, but these regions should not be regarded as universal determinants across ZYMV populations. An integrated approach combining healthy planting material, resistance deployment, surveillance, vector management and field sanitation provides a practical framework for ZYMV control. Emerging ribonucleic acid (RNA)-based, cross-protection and biological strategies have shown experimental potential but still require field validation. Ultimately, establishing a national integrated monitoring and management system that closely aligns genomics, epidemiology, and crop breeding is crucial for achieving long-term and effective control of this devastating viral disease.

title: STAP2 contributes to retinal endothelial dysfunction in diabetes through CXCR4-associated signaling revealed by single-cell RNA sequencing.
abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a leading cause of vision loss and is driven by diabetes-induced retinal endothelial dysfunction. However, diabetes-associated transcriptional heterogeneity within retinal endothelial cells (ECs) and its molecular regulators remain incompletely understood. Retinal ECs were re-analyzed from a previously published single-cell RNA sequencing dataset of db/db and db/m mouse retinas. STAP2 expression was evaluated in db/db and streptozotocin (STZ)-induced diabetic mouse retinas, human proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) tissue, and human retinal microvascular endothelial cells (HRMECs). Gain- and loss-of-function studies assessed endothelial proliferation, migration, angiogenic activity, retinal capillary degeneration, and vascular leakage. Transcriptomic profiling was used to identify downstream mediators. Three transcriptionally defined endothelial subclusters were identified, with EC3 predominantly represented in the diabetic group and showing relatively higher expression of signal-transducing adaptor protein 2 (STAP2). STAP2 was increased in diabetic retinas and high-glucose-treated HRMECs. STAP2 knockdown suppressed HRMEC proliferation, migration, and early tube formation in vitro and reduced acellular capillary formation and Evans blue extravasation in vivo, whereas STAP2 overexpression promoted these responses. Transcriptomic analysis identified C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 4 (CXCR4) as a candidate downstream mediator, and CXCR4 silencing attenuated STAP2-induced endothelial responses. These findings identify STAP2 as a previously unrecognized regulator associated with diabetic retinal endothelial dysfunction and reveal CXCR4-associated signaling as a potential mechanism involved in STAP2-mediated endothelial responses. This study provides new insights into endothelial regulation during diabetic vascular injury.

title: A Novel TEAD2 Variant Disrupts Eye Development Resulting in Microphthalmia and Ocular Coloboma.
abstract: Microphthalmia, anophthalmia, and coloboma (MAC) are caused by disrupted early eye development. Only one third of patients receive a molecular diagnosis; thus, further genomic analysis is required to identify pathogenic variants. In this study, we describe the identification of a novel heterozygous nonsense variant in TEAD2 (c.47G>A, p.Trp16Ter) in a previously unsolved family with phenotypically variable MAC. Laboratory-based study. A proband, his affected father, and unaffected mother. Stem cell-derived optic vesicles (OVs) were generated from the proband (referred to as BM), his affected father (referred to as UM) and 2 wild-type male controls aged 24 and 38 years. DNA samples from the proband and both parents underwent whole-genome sequencing and were analyzed. Zebrafish embryos were injected with tead1a/b morpholino oligomers and with synthesized human TEAD2 mRNA. Fibroblasts were derived from patients and controls and reprogrammed to induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) by episomal DNA reprogramming. The iPSCs were characterized and differentiated to OVs through an adapted protocol. Optic vesicles were characterized by Western blot, immunohistochemistry, and RNA-seq. Correction of the disease phenotype in zebrafish injected with human TEAD2 mRNA. Altered morphology and aberrant transcriptomic and proteomic profiles in patient-derived OVs due to the TEAD2 variant. RNA-seq transcriptomic analysis revealed disruptions to gene regulatory networks (GRNs) involved in eye development, and immunofluorescence studies of OVs at day 20 revealed a mislocalization of YAP1 from the nucleus to the cytoplasm. At day 35, aberrant expression of MITF and VSX2 was observed in patient OVs, suggesting disrupted vesicle patterning. Assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing revealed weaker binding at TEAD2 DNA motifs in patient OVs. The specific correction of the disease phenotype in zebrafish morphants, disruption to GRNs and abnormal expression patterns of fate-determining transcription factors in patient OVs suggests pathogenicity of the identified TEAD2 variant. Here, we present an initial report of a TEAD2 disease-causing variant and associated molecular disruptions in eye morphogenesis. Proprietary or commercial disclosure may be found in the Footnotes and Disclosures at the end of this article.

title: Circular RNAs in Hepatocellular Carcinoma: Biogenesis, Detection, Functional Mechanisms, and Translational Evidence.
abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) have been implicated in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) through microRNA-associated regulation, protein interactions, transcriptional control, and production of functional peptides. However, mechanistic activity does not establish clinical usefulness. This critical narrative review examines circRNA biogenesis, synthesis, and detection, then evaluates how selected HCC findings support proposed diagnostic and therapeutic applications. It distinguishes general RNA technologies from HCC-specific evidence and separates cell and animal experiments from human clinical validation. Representative studies are compared by circular RNA identity, molecular mechanism, experimental model, cohort design, and independent validation. The diagnostic literature includes a plasma circRNA panel evaluated in independent HBV-related cohorts, but prospective benefit beyond established surveillance remains unproven. Other candidates show prognostic or treatment-associated signals that require validation in clinically relevant populations, including patients with cirrhosis. CircRNA-SORE, circIPO11, and circPETH-147aa provide testable preclinical therapeutic hypotheses, while engineered circRNA vaccines remain supported by animal studies in the reports examined. Major priorities include reproducible junction-specific assays, confirmation of endogenous mechanisms, etiological and stage-specific validation, selective delivery, and assessment of pharmacokinetics, immunogenicity, and manufacturing consistency. CircRNAs warrant further investigation in HCC, but development should be guided by the intended clinical decision and the strength of the supporting evidence rather than by molecular association alone.

title: HSPA5-associated transcriptional programs and cellular phenotypes in follicular thyroid carcinoma.
abstract: Follicular thyroid carcinoma (FTC) is difficult to distinguish from benign follicular lesions before surgery. This study examined heat shock protein family A member 5 (HSPA5), an endoplasmic reticulum chaperone, and its association with ferroptosis-related transcriptional programs and cellular phenotypes in FTC. Five public transcriptomic cohorts were integrated for candidate discovery, external characterization, and paired-tissue evaluation. HSPA5 was silenced with two short-hairpin RNA constructs in FTC-238 and FTC-133 cells. Knockdown, metabolic activity, DNA synthesis, wound closure, migration, and invasion were evaluated using molecular and cell-based assays. In exploratory analyses, HSPA5 correlated with ferroptosis-driver and lipid-peroxidation scores (Spearman rho = 0.709 and 0.791; false-discovery rates = 0.023 and 0.013). Expression was higher in eight patient-matched primary FTC samples than in adjacent thyroid (P = 0.0078). External discrimination between FTC and follicular adenoma was limited (area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve = 0.51). In both FTC-238 and FTC-133 cells, HSPA5 silencing reduced the 24-h Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) signal and the numbers of migrating and invading cells, but increased the 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU)-positive fraction. HSPA5 is associated with ferroptosis-related transcriptional programs, and its depletion reduces 24-h CCK-8 signals and Transwell cell counts in FTC models. The role of HSPA5 in ferroptotic cell death requires functional validation.

title: Single-cell transcriptomics and machine learning identify SQLE as a candidate lipid metabolism gene associated with keratinocyte-Th17 cell crosstalk in obesity-exacerbated psoriasis.
abstract: Psoriasis is a systemic, immune-mediated inflammatory skin disease strongly associated with metabolic syndrome and obesity. While dysregulation of systemic lipid metabolism is a known exacerbating factor, the localized metabolic reprogramming within the skin microenvironment and its specific role in driving intercellular crosstalk between structural and immune cells remain largely unknown. We integrated single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) of psoriatic and normal skin with bulk transcriptomic data. Lipid metabolic activity at the single-cell level was evaluated using AUCell. To identify diagnostic hub genes, three machine learning algorithms - LASSO regression, Random Forest (RF), and Boruta - were applied to the bulk dataset. T cell subpopulation heterogeneity and intercellular communication were assessed using Seurat and CellChat. To provide preliminary validation of our bioinformatics findings in vivo, we established an obese-psoriasis mouse model using a High-Fat Diet (HFD) combined with topical Imiquimod (IMQ), evaluated via histological staining, immunohistochemistry (IHC), immunofluorescence and ELISA. ScRNA-seq analysis characterized 8 major skin cell types, revealing a significant expansion of T cells and myeloid cells in psoriatic lesions. AUCell scoring demonstrated that psoriatic keratinocytes exhibited the highest lipid metabolic activity among all cell types, with a significant elevation compared to normal controls. Machine learning on bulk transcriptomics identified four core lipid metabolism genes (SQLE, SPTLC2, PLA2G4D, and PLBD1). SQLE was significantly upregulated in psoriatic keratinocytes and demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy. The analysis of the cell communication network suggested potential communication relationships between SQLE+ keratinocytes and Th17 cells, although the identified ligand-receptor pairs were not specific to Th17 cells. In vivo verification demonstrated that diet-induced obesity significantly exacerbated the psoriasis-like lesions induced by IMQ. Immunohistochemical results showed that high expression of SQLE was located in the keratinocytes area, and the infiltration of CD4+IL17A+ Th17 cells in the dermis increased. Additionally, in the obesity-psoriasis model, ELISA test results revealed that the levels of IL-17A and TNF-α were significantly elevated. Our findings identified SQLE as a candidate molecular link between keratinocyte lipid metabolic dysfunction and Th17 cell-mediated cutaneous inflammation in the context of obesity. Our findings suggest that the SQLE-Th17 pathway is potentially hyperactivated under obese conditions, contributing to psoriasis exacerbation. Targeting SQLE and its downstream metabolic-immune communication pathways represents a promising therapeutic frontier for psoriasis patients with comorbid metabolic syndrome, pending validation through functional studies.

title: WTAP/m6A/YTHDF1-mediated upregulation of Midkine expression drives clear cell renal cell carcinoma metastasis: insights from single-cell sequencing.
abstract: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) is the most common subtype of kidney cancer. It is highly heterogeneous and exhibits a pronounced tendency towards haematogenous metastasis, which together contribute to poor overall survival. The molecular and cellular programs that distinguish metastatic from non-metastatic primary ccRCC remain incompletely defined. Here, through single-cell RNA sequencing of primary tumours from non-metastatic and metastatic ccRCC patients, we revealed marked differences in the tumour microenvironment and identified Midkine (MDK) as a molecular signature associated with ccRCC progression and poor prognosis. MDK was significantly upregulated in metastatic ccRCC, particularly in PT and dPT1 tumour cell lineages, and mediated crosstalk between tumour cells and M2-like macrophage subtypes. These macrophages in turn interacted with CD8 + T cells through SPP1 and CD24, suggesting a potential immunosuppressive mechanism. The genes upregulated in CD8 + T cells from metastatic ccRCC patients were enriched in chemokine receptor-chemokine interactions and IL-10 signalling. Mechanistically, WTAP promoted m6A methylation of MDK mRNA and increased its stability by facilitating YTHDF1 binding, thus increasing MDK protein levels and driving ccRCC cell proliferation, invasion, metastasis, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition while inhibiting apoptosis. These findings define an MDK-centred immunosuppressive axis and a WTAP/m6A/YTHDF1/MDK regulatory pathway that promotes ccRCC malignant progression, highlighting MDK as a potential prognostic biomarker and therapeutic target for metastatic ccRCC.

title: Multi-omics-guided identification of SHTN1 reveals its role in F-actin-junction remodeling and alveolar epithelial barrier integrity in acute lung injury.
abstract: Acute lung injury (ALI) and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) are characterized by diffuse alveolar damage (DAD) and disruption of the alveolar epithelial barrier, for which no targeted pharmacotherapy exists. The junction complexes maintaining this barrier depend on the cortical F-actin cytoskeleton, yet molecules linking actin organization to epithelial junctional integrity in ALI remain poorly defined. Bulk microarray, single-nucleus RNA-seq, and GeoMx spatial transcriptomic datasets were integrated to prioritize ALI-associated genes using differential expression, WGCNA, ensemble machine-learning feature selection, independent-cohort validation and Bayesian network learning. SHTN1 (Shootin1, formerly KIAA1598) was selected for mechanistic validation. Stable SHTN1 knockdown and overexpression A549 lines were evaluated in an LPS-induced in vitro model of epithelial barrier injury by transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER), FITC-dextran (4 kDa) permeability, junction-protein immunofluorescence, phalloidin staining, Western blot, and co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP), with SHTN1 reconstitution and jasplakinolide-mediated F-actin stabilization as rescue interventions. Multi-omics integration prioritized six candidate genes (BIRC5, CCR2, CENPF, GPI, SHTN1, TSTA3) from 21,124 genes; SHTN1 was pursued for its epithelial expression pattern and limited prior characterization in ALI. Single-nucleus data suggested SHTN1 enrichment in AT1 cells and reduced epithelial expression during ALI, with coordinated downregulation of cytoskeleton, morphogenesis, and adhesion pathways; spatial analysis showed exploratory downregulation of cytoskeleton- and junction-related genes in severe DAD regions. In vitro, LPS decreased SHTN1 mRNA and protein in a time- and dose-dependent manner. SHTN1 knockdown reduced monolayer barrier resistance at baseline and aggravated LPS-induced disruption, accompanied by fragmented F-actin stress fibers, discontinuous cortical actin, downregulation of FLNA, β-catenin, JUP, ITGAV, ZO-1, and E-cadherin, and a mild increase in apoptosis. Co-IP suggested SHTN1 resides in protein complexes containing β-actin and FLNA. SHTN1 overexpression was protective, and both SHTN1 reconstitution and jasplakinolide partially rescued knockdown-induced barrier and cytoskeletal defects. SHTN1 is a candidate regulator of epithelial barrier integrity in ALI. In LPS-stimulated A549 monolayers, SHTN1 deficiency was associated with F-actin disorganization, loss of junction-associated proteins, and increased epithelial permeability, which SHTN1 reconstitution and pharmacological F-actin stabilization partially reversed, indicating that a SHTN1-F-actin-junction axis may contribute to epithelial barrier dysfunction in ALI.

title: LPAR6 promoter methylation is associated with platinum resistance in ovarian cancer: a translational study integrating bioinformatics and experimental validation.
abstract: Platinum resistance remains the leading cause of treatment failure in epithelial ovarian cancer (EOC). Promoter methylation of the Lysophosphatidic Acid Receptor 6 (LPAR6) gene has been associated with poor prognosis in other malignancies, but its role in EOC chemotherapy response is unexplored. This study aimed to determine whether LPAR6 promoter methylation and expression are associated with primary platinum response in EOC. We performed a three-phase translational study. Phase I evaluated LPAR6 expression using TCGA-OV RNA-seq data (n = 235). Phase II quantified LPAR6 promoter methylation using RRBS data from an independent cohort (GSE102119; n = 16, comprising 8 sensitive and 8 resistant cases). The cohorts were independent without paired patient-level data. Phase III validated findings in ovarian cancer cell lines by qRT-PCR, methylation-specific PCR, 5-Aza rescue, Western blotting, and MTT assays. Phase I showed no significant difference in LPAR6 expression between sensitive and resistant patients (P = 0.752; AUC = 0.507). Phase II revealed substantially higher promoter methylation in resistant tumors (0.67 vs 0.36; P < 0.001; AUC = 0.95). This finding is exploratory due to limited sample size. Phase III confirmed LPAR6 expression was significantly lower in resistant cell lines (P < 0.01), methylation was exclusive to resistant cells, 5-Aza restored LPAR6 expression (2.8-3.5 fold, P < 0.01), and LPAR6 protein was downregulated in resistant cells. LPAR6 expression alone was not associated with platinum response. However, promoter methylation showed strong association with resistance, validated experimentally. Within the translational research framework, these exploratory findings establish a foundation for future clinical validation studies. Prospective validation in larger cohorts with predefined methylation cut-offs is warranted before clinical implementation.
